records.why: The rhythmic-clapping method only works if the round-trip time 2d/v is long enough to clap to. At 20 m it is 40 ÷ 340 = 0.118 s (about 8.5 claps per second), at 30 m 0.176 s (5.7 per second): not possible by hand. At 40 m it is 0.235 s (4.3 per second) and at 80 m 0.47 s (2.1 per second): workable. The phone-recorder option is added for schools without a long wall. Checked twice by recomputing 2d/v for each distance.

Each group is assigned one distance: Group A = 40 m, Group B = 50 m, Group C = 60 m, Group D = 70 m, Group E = 80 m (use the longest distances your field allows, but never less than 40 m: at 20 m the echo returns after only about 0.12 s, so a learner would have to clap about 8 times a second to keep in time with it, which is impossible; at 40 m it is about 4 claps a second, which is possible with practice or with two wooden blocks). Diffraction does not carry FM or mobile signals round big hills or from Nairobi to Kisumu. Wavelengths of about 0.17 m (1.8 GHz phone) to 3 m (98.4 MHz FM) are far smaller than a hill, so there is very little diffraction and a signal shadow forms (which is what the matatu passenger hears). Nairobi-to-Kisumu reception uses relay transmitters, not diffraction. The old prompts also contradicted Problem 1 in the same lesson (a 3 m wave diffracts poorly round a 200 m hill). Checked: 3.0e8/98.4e6 = 3.05 m; 3.0e8/1.8e9 = 0.167 m.

records.new: (2) 'The signal on my phone or FM radio fades when I go behind a big hill near Nakuru/Kericho because the wavelength of the signal is only about ___ m, much smaller than the hill, so…' (3) 'A radio station can still be heard in a faraway town such as Kisumu, even though the Earth curves, because…' (hint: relay transmitters repeat the signal, and long-wavelength AM waves spread round obstacles and follow the Earth's curve better than FM).
records.reference: OpenStax University Physics Vol. 3, Chapter 4 (Diffraction: effect is significant only when wavelength is comparable to the obstacle or opening size)

records.why: Knock-on of the diffraction/radio fix: the lesson now teaches that short waves diffract little round big hills.
records.old: (c) The microwaves of the phone signal diffract around the hill, but only imperfectly, so the signal is weak or fades in the valley behind. Engineers place repeater towers on hilltops to boost the signal into the valleys.
records.new: (c) The microwaves of the phone signal have a wavelength of only about 0.17 m, much smaller than the hill, so they diffract very little and a signal shadow forms behind the hill; the signal is weak or fades in the valley. Engineers place relay towers on hilltops or in the valley to bring the signal round the hill.

Lesson 5 plans about 97 minutes for an 80-minute double period: the doorway experiment alone is 25 minutes while the teacher notes allow each group 4 minutes at one doorway (8 groups x 4 = 32 minutes). Using two doorways with 2-minute turns makes Part A about 15 minutes, the simulation 8 minutes, and Problem 2 homework, which brings the lesson to about 78 minutes.
records.old: PART A — Doorway Sound Experiment (25 minutes). The class divides into groups of 5. Each group takes a turn at the open classroom doorway; the rest observe and record. Within each group: one learner (the 'speaker') stands 0.5 m outside the doorway and claps twice or says a short phrase ('Habari za asubuhi!') at normal conversational volume; two learners (listeners L1 and L2) stand around the corner in the corridor at 1 m and 2 m from the doorway edge respectively, both out of the speaker's line of sight; one learner acts as the 'control listener' (L3) who stands in the direct line of sight of the speaker at 1 m, confirming sound is audible in the direct path; one learner records results in a class results table on the board. Each group tests three conditions: (i) doorway fully open (gap ≈ 1 m wide); (ii) doorway half-blocked with a book or bag (gap ≈ 0.5 m); (iii) doorway almost fully blocked (gap ≈ 0.1 m, leaving a narrow slit). Listeners rate audibility as 3 (clear), 2 (faint), or 1 (cannot hear). Results are compiled in a shared class table. After all groups rotate, learners write two observations in their exercise books: 'What happened to the sound around the corner?' and 'What happened as the gap got narrower?' PART B — Water-Wave Diffraction Simulation (10 minutes)
records.new: PART A — Doorway Sound Experiment (15 minutes). The class divides into groups of 5. Two doorways (front and back door) are used at the same time, and each group takes a 2-minute turn at one of them; the rest observe and record. Within each group: one learner (the 'speaker') stands 0.5 m outside the doorway and claps twice or says a short phrase ('Habari za asubuhi!') at normal conversational volume; two learners (listeners L1 and L2) stand around the corner in the corridor at 1 m and 2 m from the doorway edge respectively, both out of the speaker's line of sight; one learner acts as the 'control listener' (L3) who stands in the direct line of sight of the speaker at 1 m, confirming sound is audible in the direct path; one learner records results in a class results table on the board. Each group tests three conditions: (i) doorway fully open (gap ≈ 1 m wide); (ii) doorway half-blocked with a book or bag (gap ≈ 0.5 m); (iii) doorway almost fully blocked (gap ≈ 0.1 m, leaving a narrow slit). Listeners rate audibility as 3 (clear), 2 (faint), or 1 (cannot hear). Results are compiled in a shared class table. After all groups rotate, learners write two observations in their exercise books: 'What happened to the sound around the corner?' and 'What happened as the gap got narrower?' PART B — Water-Wave Diffraction Simulation (8 minutes)
